title: Simple Dash Cams for Everyday Drivers: How They Work, What They Cost, and the Rules to Know
subtitle: A plain-English guide to small car cameras, the memory cards they need, and the windshield and audio rules that vary by state.
excerpt: A dash cam quietly records the road while you drive, which can help sort out what happened after a fender bender. Here is how loop recording works, what to budget for, and what to check before you mount one.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: Most of us have had a close call in a parking lot, or a disagreement after a minor bump about who backed into whom. In those moments, it is your word against theirs. A dash cam is a small camera that sits on your windshield and records the road ahead while you drive, so there is a video record if you ever need one.

It is worth being clear about what a dash cam cannot do. It records; it does not prevent a crash, stop a break-in, or call for help in a medical emergency. It is not a car safety system or a medical alert. If you or a passenger is hurt, call 911.

A dash cam saves video onto a microSD card, the tiny fingernail-sized memory card used in many cameras. A card can only hold so much, so the camera records in short chunks, called loops. When the card fills up, the camera records over the oldest chunks first.

In an older Consumer Reports article, about six years old, the advice is to choose a longer loop length, and it says 5 minutes is better than the minimum. It is a good reminder to check what loop lengths a camera offers. Among the cameras below, the Garmin Mini 3 lists a G-sensor (a sensor that feels sudden jolts) and automatic incident detection.
"You need a loop file that's at least 3 minutes long." — Consumer Reports, "What to Look for in an Aftermarket Dash Cam"

One catch: without a card, or with a worn-out one, nothing gets saved at all. The Garmin Mini 3 does not come with a card, and the specs for the VIOFO do not show one in the box either, so plan to buy one.

items: Simple controls. Some cameras have no screen and are run by voice commands or a phone app. That keeps them small, but you will need a smartphone to watch clips.
Front only or front and rear. A single front camera covers most needs. A front-and-rear set also records out the back window, but the extra camera means more installation work.
The memory card. Check the camera's manual for the maximum card size it accepts, and add the card to your budget.
Subscriptions. No monthly fee is shown on the pages for the cameras below, but a retailer listing says Garmin's cloud sharing and remote parking alerts need a paid plan. Confirm before you buy.
Power. The easiest setup uses the adhesive mount and plugs into the car's lighter socket. Wiring into the fuse box, or any installation near an airbag, is a job for a shop.
Setup help. Ask whether installation is offered, as Best Buy does in store for the Garmin.

sections.content: Mounting It and Using It Well

State law generally bars anything on the front windshield that blocks the driver's view, but the exact rules on placement differ. Sources even disagree on details: one says Texas allows the top 5 inches, while another says New York allows only behind-the-mirror placement. Check your own state's rules before you stick anything to the glass, since adhesive mounts are hard to move once placed.

Audio is the other thing to think about. Several states require everyone in the car to agree before a conversation is recorded, and sources give different counts, so check your own state's law. If your passengers have not agreed, turn the microphone off.
Once it is up, format the memory card in the camera itself (this prepares the card, and the option is in the camera's settings or app). Also check the card's maximum size in the manual.

Budget beyond the camera. The Garmin Mini 3 does not include a memory card, and Best Buy sells its constant power cable separately for $49.99. Garmin's cloud sharing may also require a subscription. Prices change with holiday sales, so check the price on the day you buy.
sections.label: Before You Buy

sections.content: A dash cam can be a useful extra record of a drive, as long as you keep its card in good shape. Pick a simple one, give it a suitable memory card, and mount it where it will not block your view. Safe travels.

products.name: Garmin Dash Cam Mini 3
products.price: $149.99 on Garmin's page; $99.99 at Best Buy in a Black Friday sale. Check current price.
products.blurb: A good fit for drivers who want something small and simple: it records 1080p video with a wide 140-degree view and a Clarity polarizer to reduce glare. It has no screen, is controlled by voice or phone app, uses an adhesive mount, and needs a microSD card bought separately (at least 8 GB, Class 10 or faster).

products.name: VIOFO A229 Pro 2CH
products.price: $349.99 on VIOFO's page, where a Black Friday banner says it saves up to $110. Check current price.
products.blurb: For drivers who want both the road ahead and the road behind on video: it pairs a 4K front camera with a 2K rear camera, plus GPS and voice control. Loop length can be set to Off, 1, 2, 3, 5 or 10 minutes. VIOFO is a smaller brand, so verify availability, and consider professional installation for the rear camera.

products.name: SanDisk 64GB Ultra PLUS microSD Memory Card
products.price: $34.99 at Best Buy; Best Buy's Garmin Mini 3 page showed it at $21.99. Check current price.
products.blurb: A 64 GB microSDXC card for anyone whose dash cam came without one. Confirm that it meets your camera's requirements before buying; for the Garmin Mini 3, that means Class 10 or faster.

products.name: Car-Vue 1080P Dash Cam
products.blurb: A 1080P dash camera with a wide-angle lens, loop recording and motion detection, so there is a record if something happens on the road or in a parking lot.
